newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamists threatened with party ban.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamists threatened with party ban.

text.p: Turkey's security apparatus on Wednesday fired its biggest gun yet in a tough war of attrition against the beleaguered Islamists of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.

The country's top prosecutor Vural Savas said he had filed a case with the constitutional court to outlaw Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party on the grounds that it endangered the basic tenets of the secularist Turkish state.
The prospect of a court battle gave Erbakan's coalition government no respite after it struggled on Tuesday to fend off the toughest parliamentary challenge yet to its 11-month-old rule.

"It has become clear that (Welfare) has become a focus of actions contrary to the principle of secularism in the constitution and has pushed our country towards a civil war atmosphere," said Savas, quoting the 18-page charge sheet.
Investor reaction was muted, with Istanbul stocks closing down 0.07 percent. Legal sources said it could take at least six months for a verdict in any court case aimed at closing Welfare.
Erbakan has upset the secularist elite, led by the army, with plans for limited Islamist reforms since he became NATO member Turkey's first Islamist leader in modern times last June.
The prime minister rejected the prosecutor's charges. "It is a simple accusation that has nothing to do with the truth," he told reporters.
The pro-Western generals also criticise Erbakan for courting Iran and Syria, accused by the army of sponsoring Turkish Kurd separatist rebels.

Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency said on Wednesday that Syrian, Iraqi and Iranian troops had built up near the borders of a Kurdish enclave in northern Iraq to aid guerrillas fleeing a Turkish army incursion there.
Most of the fractious opposition united briefly on Tuesday in a secularist bid to topple Erbakan that fell short by only half-a-dozen votes in the 550-seat parliament.
The government, hit by desertions among MPs in its secularist wing, was saved by six deputies from a small far-right party who voted for Erbakan.
Prosecutor Savas said the government was trying to destroy the secularist system set up by leader Kemal Ataturk in the 1920s after the fall of the religion-based Ottoman Empire.
"Even if some of our politicians are deluded, manipulative or involved in treason, the republic of Turkey established by the great Ataturk will live on," Savas said.
He cited fiery speeches by Erbakan and other Welfare members that he said were calls for sharia Islamic law to be imposed on Turkey, if necessary by violence.

Turkey's security forces do not face any serious threat from armed Islamist groups. But the army, which has carried out three coups since 1960, says its fight against Islamism is a matter of "life or death".
Police have closed dozens of illegal Islamic education centres in recent weeks in line with an army request.
Two Kurdish political factions have been outlawed by the constitutional court in recent years for alleged separatism but their members have later formed new parties and regrouped.
The main opposition Motherland Party gave Erbakan lukewarm support against the court action.

"It would be preferable to take action inside parliament," prominent Motherland deputy Murat Basesgioglu told private NTV television. He said his party would soon bring a fresh censure motion -- four earlier ones failed -- to oust the government.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, the head of the True Path Party coalition partner, held talks on Tuesday with potential rebel backbenchers to convince them not to ditch the government.
